output_text: Anyone who compares a field of cultivated wheat with a stand of wild grass will see that the crop plants vary more among themselves than the wild ones do. Livestock show the same pattern: two dairy cows from the same herd can differ in size, color, temperament, and yield far more than two deer from the same forest. This is not a coincidence, and it is not simply the result of breeders picking out odd individuals. The variation seems to come from the conditions under which domesticated species live. A wild population faces a fairly stable set of pressures over long stretches of time. A cultivated one is moved between climates, fed on new diets, sheltered from predators, and bred in ways that would never happen on its own, and those changes in circumstance appear to loosen whatever holds a species to its typical form. Some researchers have suggested that a rich food supply plays a particular role. That seems plausible, though it is hard to separate from everything else that changes when an animal is brought under human care. What is clearer is that the effect takes time to appear and does not readily switch off. A species may need to live for several generations under new conditions before it starts producing noticeable variants, but once it does, it tends to keep producing them. Even our oldest crops continue to throw off new strains, and our oldest domestic animals are still being reshaped by breeders today.
notes: The source attributes the food-supply idea to "some researchers" without naming any; I kept the attribution as written, and it needs a citation before this is published.

output_text: I was born on a small farm outside a market town in eastern Maryland. I cannot say exactly when. No one wrote it down, or if they did, I never saw the record. That was the ordinary situation for enslaved people in that part of the country. Most of them could not have told you the year of their birth, let alone the day, and the men who owned them preferred it that way. Dates were kept for livestock and account books, not for people who were themselves entered in the account book. When someone did try to place a birth, they used the seasons: around planting, around harvest, the year the cherries came in early. As a child this bothered me more than I could explain. The white children knew how old they were and said so freely. I did not understand what made my case different, and I was not permitted to ask. My owner treated any question of that kind as a sign of insolence, the first symptom of a slave who was thinking too much. My best guess now is that I am in my late twenties. I arrived at that figure only because I once overheard my owner mention my age in passing, and I have been counting forward from it ever since.

My father was physically sound, of average height but solidly built and unusually strong. He had a range of small talents that he never made much of. He could sketch well, knew enough music to play a few hymns on the fiddle, and had a good singing voice, so on evenings when the shop was closed he would sometimes play and sing for the family, which we all enjoyed. He was also handy in a general way and could pick up almost any tradesman's tools and use them competently.

People valued his judgment most. He had a practical, level-headed way of thinking about problems, whether domestic or public, and neighbors came to rely on it. He never held any office, because with a large family to support and not much money he could not afford time away from his trade. Even so, I remember prominent men from the town and from his congregation calling at the house to ask his view on some matter under discussion, and listening to his answer with real attention. Private individuals brought him their disputes too, and he was often asked to arbitrate between parties who could not settle a quarrel on their own.

The simplest way to understand what government is for is to imagine a situation without one. Picture a handful of people who have landed in some remote place, cut off from every other society. They stand in for the first inhabitants of any country. The first thing they will do, before anyone thinks about rules or leaders, is form a community, because none of them can manage alone. One person's needs run far ahead of one person's strength, and few people can stand extended isolation. Each of them will look for help from the others, and each will be asked for help in return.

Consider the practical problem of building shelter. Four or five people working together can put up a decent cabin in a clearing within a season. A single person could spend an entire lifetime and never finish. He might cut down the trees, but he could not haul the logs, and if he somehow hauled them, he could not raise them into walls by himself. In the meantime he has to eat, so hunting or gathering interrupts the work every day, and every new need drags him off in another direction. If he falls ill or breaks a leg, he is finished. The injury itself would not kill him, but it would stop him from doing the work that keeps him alive.

Most of us worry far more than our circumstances require. We could hand off a good share of the care we lavish on ourselves and lose nothing by it, since the world is built to accommodate our weak points as well as our strong ones. For some people, constant anxiety has become a chronic condition that no amount of reassurance seems to cure. Part of the problem is that we overrate the importance of our own work. Look at how much gets done without us. If we were laid up for a month, things would mostly carry on. Yet we stay on guard all day, refusing to trust anything we cannot control, and only at night, worn out, do we reluctantly let go and accept that the next day is uncertain. We are so committed to living the way we live that we treat our habits as sacred and cannot imagine doing otherwise. This is the only way, we tell ourselves. But there are as many ways to live as there are directions to walk from a single point. Change looks like a miracle from the outside, and yet it is happening all the time, in small increments, to everyone. Real knowledge, as an old proverb puts it, is knowing what you know and knowing what you do not. Once one person has turned a hope into a fact, sooner or later everyone builds on it.
notes: The source attributes its quotation to "an old proverb" without naming one, and its last two sentences do not connect to the argument about worry; I kept both in place, and the ending needs a link to the anxiety argument or a cut.

By the time I could read the river the way I could read a page, and knew every bend and snag and sandbar along it by heart, I had gained a skill that would earn me a living. But the skill had a permanent cost. The river stopped being beautiful to me.

I can still remember a particular sunset from my first weeks on the water, before any of that had happened. The whole surface of the river had gone red, fading to gold in the middle distance, and a single dark log drifted through the gold like a stroke of ink. Off to one side a long slanting streak caught the light and sparkled. Somewhere else the water churned in slow rings that shifted through every color you could name. Where the red was palest there was a patch of glassy water marked with faint circles and radiating lines, as if someone had drawn them with a fine pen. The left bank was heavy forest, and the shadow it threw across the water was cut in one place by a bright ruffled path that looked like beaten silver. Above the treeline a dead tree with a single living branch stood against the sky, and that branch caught the last full light of the sun and seemed to burn. There were curves and reflections, wooded bluffs, softened distances, and over all of it the light kept shifting as the sun went down, so that every minute the scene rearranged itself into something new. I had never seen anything like it, and at the time I did not know that I was looking at it for the last time in that way.
